items.title: White Gi Fighter Blends with Background
items.what: In the gameplay view (e.g., Image 3, 4), the player character 'Asmongold' (white gi) stands directly in front of bright, glowing shoji screen windows. The white of the gi and the character's skin tone have very low contrast against the bright yellow/white background panels, making the limb positions and animations difficult to distinguish.
items.why: Visual clarity is critical in a fighting game. If a player cannot clearly see their own character's silhouette or limb extension against the background, they cannot judge spacing, timing, or whether an attack connected, leading to frustration and perceived unfairness.
items.how: Implement a dynamic lighting adjustment that slightly darkens the specific background window panels directly behind the fighters, or add a subtle, dark rim-light shader to the white gi sprite to separate it from the bright background.

items.title: Countdown Timer Looks Like a Clickable Button
items.what: On the pre-fight screen (Image 2, 11) and game-over screen (Image 8), the countdown element ('FIGHT IN 2', 'REMATCH IN 8') is styled as a glossy, gold, pill-shaped button with beveled edges, identical to interactive UI elements.
items.why: This creates a 'false affordance.' Players will instinctively try to tap it to skip the wait or start the match early. When nothing happens, it feels unresponsive. It confuses the visual language of the UI.
items.how: Change the visual style of the countdown to be non-interactive. Remove the button bevel/gloss and use simple, large typography, or replace it with a circular progress ring that depletes, clearly signaling 'wait' rather than 'click'.

items.title: In-Game Control Legend is Misleading
items.what: The text legend above the joysticks (Image 3, 10) lists simple single-direction inputs for Techniques ('back', 'forward', 'up', 'down'). However, the 'Techniques' menu (Image 6) reveals that moves require complex combinations (e.g., 'Back + Forward' for Back Fist, 'Up + Forward' for Jumping Punch).
items.why: The on-screen legend teaches the player incorrect information. A player following the legend will never discover the special moves because they aren't told that chorded inputs or sequences are possible. This hides the depth of the combat system.
items.how: Remove the static text legend entirely to save screen space. Instead, rely on the 'LUNGE PUNCH' notification (Image 5) to teach moves as they are performed, or add a 'Last Move' hint bubble near the joystick that shows the input combination just used.

items.title: Techniques Reference List is Too Dense
items.what: The 'TECHNIQUES' modal (Image 6) is a wall of text with very small directional icons (circles with arrows) and small font sizes. The distinction between similar moves (e.g., 'Lunge Punch' vs 'Stepping Lunge Punch') relies on spotting tiny differences in the icon sequence.
items.why: Players need to reference this list to learn the game. If it is difficult to read on a mobile screen, they will not learn the advanced moves, reducing the game's longevity and skill ceiling. It feels like a spreadsheet rather than a game menu.
items.how: Increase the size of the directional icons by 50%. Use color coding for the stick directions (e.g., Green for Forward, Red for Back) to make the patterns scannable. Group moves by 'type' (Punches, Kicks) rather than just stick direction to aid memorization.

items.title: Camera Does Not Reframe for Landscape Orientation
items.what: In the landscape screenshot (Image 9), the game renders, but the camera framing remains identical to the portrait view. This results in the fighters appearing tiny in the center of the screen with massive amounts of empty dojo space on the left and right.
items.why: While portrait is the baseline, players may rotate their phones. Currently, landscape mode is practically unplayable because the fighters are too small to see details, and the touch controls are stretched into uncomfortable corners. It wastes the screen real estate.
items.how: Detect landscape orientation and trigger a camera zoom (or FOV reduction) that fills the vertical height of the screen with the fighters, similar to the portrait framing. Alternatively, lock the game to portrait orientation if landscape support is not a priority.
